an0193.user: Running Google Performance Max for my eyewear brand, last 30 days. AOV is sitting around ₹1,300, margins about 54%, and CAC is ₹401 so my ROAS is a clean 3.2. CTR's healthy at 2.6%. Honestly the ads look like they're printing money — I want to pour more budget in. Any reason not to?

One caveat — 9% over 90 days on a young brand can partly be a window problem; some of those buyers will reorder in month 4-6. Pull the 180-day number before you decide how bad the leak really is. But even generously, this is a retention problem, not an acquisition one.

an0198.user: Home-care brand, selling mostly through WhatsApp broadcast. I've been at this 4 weeks and my CAC is ₹436 which feels high. AOV is ₹1,000, ROAS about 2.3, CTR's fine at 2.3%. My margin is 27%. I keep trying to get the CAC down but it's stubborn. How do I lower my CAC?

You're aiming at the wrong number. Lowering CAC won't save this — let me show you why with your own figures.

Contribution per order = ₹1,000 × 27% − ₹436 = ₹270 − ₹436 = −₹166. Every order you ship loses you ₹166 before you've spent a single rupee on overheads, salaries or that WhatsApp tooling. So even if you fought CAC down from ₹436 to, say, ₹350, you'd still be at −₹80. You can't market your way out of this; the hole is structural.

The disease is the 27% gross margin. On a ₹1,000 order that leaves only ₹270 to cover the entire cost of acquiring the customer — and ₹270 is just too thin a slab to buy a customer profitably on paid media. The CAC isn't high, your margin is low, and they look like the same problem from where you're standing.

So the lever is margin, not ads: get COGS down, or push AOV up (bundles, a premium SKU, a refill subscription so the second order costs you almost nothing to acquire), or reprice. Move gross margin from 27% toward ~45% and suddenly ₹436 CAC is workable.

Caveat — if WhatsApp is partly organic and that ₹436 only reflects the paid slice, your blended economics may be softer than this. Pull blended CAC across all your acquisition before you reprice. But the direction is clear: this is a margin problem in a marketing costume.

an0199.user: Pet-care D2C, here's the dump — PMax, last 30 days, spend ₹13L, AOV ₹3,100, margin 68%, CAC ₹2,042, ROAS 1.5, CTR 2.0%, 90-day repeat 34%. That ROAS of 1.5 is terrifying me, everyone says you need 3x+ to be healthy. What's wrong, should I cut spend?

One caveat — that +₹66 is a thin cushion, so as you scale watch CAC closely; if it drifts past ~₹2,100 you tip negative on order one and start leaning entirely on repeat to bail you out. Scale, but keep a hand on the CAC dial.

an0201.user: Run a gym, been doing Meta for a while. Over the last 6 weeks my CAC went from ₹523 to ₹1,091 — basically doubled. ROAS slid from 2.3 to 1.1. AOV's ₹1,200, margin 56%. an0203.user: Home-care brand, Google Search, last 30 days. Pasting the funnel: impressions 12.5 lakh, clicks 21,410, CTR 1.7%, orders 202, conversion rate 0.94%, AOV ₹1,350. We're on broad-match keywords. The traffic is huge but sales aren't keeping up — what's wrong?
an0203.assistant:
Your funnel isn't leaking at the top — it's letting the wrong people in. The tell is the gap between two numbers: 21,410 clicks but only 202 orders, a 0.94% conversion rate. Under 1% on Google Search is the signature of low-intent traffic, not a landing-page or pricing problem.

And the cause is sitting right in your setup: broad-match keywords. Broad match is a firehose — it matches your ads to anything loosely related, so you're paying for 'how to clean a sofa' DIY-searchers, students doing research, people who'll never buy a thing. They click (hence the healthy 1.7% CTR and the 12.5 lakh impressions), they browse, they leave. You're buying curiosity, not purchase intent.

So this isn't a CTR or creative problem — CTR is fine. It's an intent problem, and the lever is to stop optimising for clicks and start filtering for buyers: tighten broad match to phrase/exact on your genuinely commercial keywords, pour in a serious negative-keyword list to choke off the informational and DIY queries, and let the high-intent terms breathe. You'll see clicks fall and conversion rate rise — that's the system working, not breaking.

Caveat: confirm conversion tracking is firing correctly before you act — a broken tag also shows as a fake-low conversion rate, and you'd hate to gut your keywords chasing a measurement bug. But assuming tracking's clean, this is classic broad-match intent dilution.

an0204.user: Jewellery brand, running Meesho Ads, ₹12.5L spend last month, post-iOS. Here's my headache — Meesho's own dashboard tells me ROAS is 4.1, but my Shopify last-click report says 1.9. The two numbers won't agree and I genuinely can't tell which one is real. Which dashboard do I believe?
an0204.assistant:
Neither, fully — and that's the actual answer, not a dodge. You're refereeing two scoreboards that are designed to disagree and will never reconcile.

Here's why. The platform's 4.1 is inflated: it counts modelled conversions and claims credit on a 7-day-click (and view-through) window, so it grabs every sale it can plausibly attach to an ad it served. Shopify's last-click 1.9 is deflated the other way: it hands all the credit to whatever the customer clicked last — usually a branded search or a direct visit — so it systematically under-credits the Meesho ad that first sparked the discovery. Post-iOS the platform side leans even harder on modelling. The truth sits somewhere between 1.9 and 4.1, and no amount of staring will make either dashboard confess to it.

So stop trying to pick a winner between two biased referees. The lever is to anchor on a number neither platform can spin: blended CAC. Take your total spend across everything ÷ the actual count of new customers Shopify recorded that month, and manage the business to that. On ₹12.5L, if you acquired, say, 900 genuinely new customers, that's a blended CAC of ~₹1,389 — a real, controllable figure. Set your target CAC against your contribution per order and steer by that.

Caveat: use NEW customers, not total orders, or repeat buyers will flatter the number. Once blended CAC is your North Star, the 4.1-vs-1.9 fight stops mattering.

an0205.user: Kids-coding edtech here. Narrow question — why does my reported ROAS look low? Meta-side it's 3.6 but my Shopify last-click shows 1.9 on ₹5L spend, last 30 days, post-iOS. Which one should I be reporting to my board?

Shopify's last-click 1.9 is stingy: it gives all the credit to the final touch — usually a branded search or direct visit — and under-credits the ad that actually planted the idea weeks earlier, which matters a lot in edtech where parents research for ages before enrolling. The number to take to your board is blended CAC: total spend ÷ actual new customers from Shopify. On ₹5L, if that bought, say, 250 genuinely new enrolments, that's ₹2,000 blended CAC — a figure no platform can inflate and you can hold yourself accountable to month over month. Pair it with contribution per enrolment and you've got an honest scorecard.

Caveat: count NEW customers only, and run blended CAC against your true LTV — edtech often monetises across multiple courses, so a 'high' CAC can still be fine if the second and third course follow. But stop reporting platform ROAS as truth; anchor the board on blended CAC.
